title: District VIII Candidates Talk Water, Infrastructure and Downtown at City Hall Forum
excerpt: Four of the six candidates for the remainder of the Laredo City Council District VIII term took part in a Nov. 12 forum at City Hall, discussing water supply, infrastructure and downtown revitalization ahead of the Dec. 5 special election, according to the Laredo Morning Times.
content:
Four of the six candidates for the remainder of the Laredo City Council District VIII term took part in a forum on Nov. 12, 2026, at City Hall, discussing water supply, infrastructure and downtown revitalization, according to the Laredo Morning Times.

The forum was part of the Laredo Votes 2026 voter-education campaign. Candidates had two minutes each for opening and closing statements and two minutes to answer four questions from media members, the newspaper reported.

The candidates who attended were Irma Morales Lopez, Oscar “Ram” Ramirez, Mario Treviño and Priscilla “Gordiloca” Treviño. José Sergio Dorantes and José Luis Maldonado did not attend; according to the newspaper, they missed the mandatory candidate orientation and therefore could not participate.

Lopez, a 33-year educator and lifelong District VIII resident, presented herself as a listener and problem-solver, the newspaper reported. She said water, infrastructure, safety and downtown were major concerns, and said that in her first year she would focus on improving quality of life and planning projects together rather than piecemeal, noting that projects often start before completion and costs rise. She called for clear priorities, deadlines and follow-through. For downtown, she supported better lighting, sidewalks, cleanliness, public safety and incentives to attract businesses and investment, and she questioned the future of the downtown business improvement tax and how dedicated money would be used.

Ramirez, who has 30 years in public service including public water, economic development and city management, emphasized communication and transparency, including monthly meetings or town halls across the district to discuss council agendas and district concerns and gather feedback before major decisions, according to the newspaper. On drainage and water infrastructure, he said he would work with department heads and subject-matter experts to identify priorities, develop long-term funding plans and ensure continued maintenance and follow-through. For downtown, he proposed reviewing existing plans, identifying funding and studying successful redevelopment programs elsewhere.

Treviño, whose background includes law enforcement, youth services and the City of Laredo Utilities Department, said he had firsthand experience with water lines and meters. He said his first priority would be meeting residents to identify pressing needs rather than assuming them, and gathering input on infrastructure, lighting, parks and other city services, working with the rest of the council across districts. For downtown, he called for coordination among city departments, including code enforcement, Solid Waste and health inspection, to address abandoned and deteriorating properties, improve lighting and pedestrian access and encourage business investment. He said state and federal funding could help spur investment and acquire or renovate vacant properties, and he mentioned grant writers. Treviño, who was born and raised in the Los Amores area, said he would make no promises but would work hard, listen and be transparent.

Priscilla Treviño, described by the newspaper as a community advocate rather than a career politician, centered her remarks on overlooked residents, older residents, people experiencing homelessness and working families. She cited water infrastructure, street lighting, downtown buildings and conditions at the Hamilton Hotel. Her first-year goals were to seek funding or formal commitments for at least three District VIII improvements, including reliable water and sewer service, better living conditions for older residents and downtown redevelopment, and to work with community partners on homelessness. On water, she said the issue had built up over years and would take decades — more than 20 years — to fix, and rejected the idea that a candidate could solve it quickly.

The special election is Dec. 5, 2026, with early voting Nov. 23 through Dec. 1, according to the newspaper.

Source: Laredo Morning Times, Nov. 14, 2026.
